# XCoT-VLA: Executable Chain-of-Thought for Vision-Language-Action Driving

- **Authors**: Foundation Model Team, XPeng Inc
- **Venue**: cs.AI
- **Published**: 2026-08-11
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10976>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.10976v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-training, test-time-scaling
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-training 0.50, test-time-scaling 0.50

## In one line

Replaces a verbose natural-language rationale with two to six executable action tokens drawn from a fixed vocabulary, supervised automatically by pairing logged trajectories with scene context, so that driving-oriented reasoning fits inside a real-time control budget that verbose chain-of-thought exceeds by three to four times.

## Problem

Vision-language-action models can connect scene understanding, semantic reasoning and trajectory generation, but a verbose natural-language chain of thought is badly suited to real-time control. It is open-ended, so its length cannot be bounded; it is costly to decode, so it competes with the control loop for latency; and it is hard to optimise as an action-facing representation, because nothing connects the words to the trajectory that has to be produced. The question is whether the reasoning can be compressed without losing what it contributes.

## Contributions

- An executable reasoning interface of two to six action tokens replacing an open-ended natural-language rationale, which bounds the reasoning length by construction rather than by a budget imposed afterwards.
- Automatic Reason-Action supervision derived by pairing logged trajectories with scene context, so the token sequence for a scene is constructed from driving logs rather than annotated.
- Deterministic token-function routing sending reasoning tokens and trajectory queries through separate feed-forward paths while sharing multimodal self-attention, so the reasoning conditions the trajectory without being generated by the same head that produces it.
- The controlled comparison against verbose chain of thought and continuous latent tokens on the same backbone, showing verbose reasoning degrades lateral accuracy below no reasoning at all on the general set while improving longitudinal accuracy.
- A latency analysis against an explicit real-time budget, measuring inter-token cost and reporting worst-case interface latency at each method's maximum output length across four input lengths, with the scope of what it excludes stated.

## Method

Descriptive rationales are replaced by compact executable tokens from a designed vocabulary of manoeuvre primitives, including symmetric pairs so that mirror-image manoeuvres share structure. Supervision for those tokens is constructed automatically rather than annotated: logged trajectories supply the action evidence for what was actually done, and the surrounding scene context supplies the causal semantics for why, so a Reason-Action pair can be derived from driving logs at scale. The predicted token sequence stays in context and conditions a fixed set of trajectory queries through shared multimodal self-attention, and a deterministic token-function routing sends the reasoning tokens through a Reason feed-forward network and the trajectory queries through a Control one, with trajectories generated by flow matching. An optional reinforcement-learning refinement operates in the same executable token space rather than over natural language. Evaluation is open-loop on a general-distribution set and a lane-change set, reporting average and final displacement error separately for lateral and longitudinal components over a six-second horizon, against three controlled variants sharing the same backbone: trajectory-only supervised fine-tuning, verbose natural-language chain of thought, and continuous latent tokens. A separate ablation on a controlled lane-change diagnostic split -- which the authors mark as not numerically comparable with the main table -- separates the contribution of the executable reasoning from that of targeted navigation data. Latency is analysed by measuring inter-token decoding cost on an H100 and computing worst-case reasoning-interface latency at each method's maximum output length against a 12 Hz planning budget.

## Results

The executable interface is best on every reported metric of both evaluation sets. On the general set, longitudinal average displacement error falls from 1.6452 to 1.3233 and final displacement error from 4.3541 to 3.0887 against trajectory-only supervision; on the lane-change set, lateral average error falls from 0.5941 to 0.3091 and lateral final error from 1.6160 to 0.6484 -- roughly a 60 percent reduction, and much larger than the longitudinal gains, which the authors read as executable reasoning being specifically effective for route-conditioned lateral decisions. The comparison against verbose chain of thought contains the paper's most useful negative result and it is reported plainly: on the general set, verbose reasoning improves both longitudinal metrics while making both lateral metrics worse than no reasoning at all (0.2609 to 0.2798 average, 0.7352 to 0.7822 final). Continuous latent tokens land between the two throughout, better than verbose reasoning but behind the executable vocabulary. The ablation on the diagnostic split localises the effect the same way: the executable reasoning alone cuts lateral average error by 18.3 percent and lateral final error by 25.1 percent while leaving both longitudinal metrics fractionally worse (1.8221 to 1.8418, 4.8399 to 4.8458), and adding targeted navigation supervision improves lateral further. So the mechanism is route-conditioned intent rather than trajectory quality in general, and the paper says so. On latency, inter-token decoding costs 3.25 ms, so a verbose rationale of 40 to 80 tokens gives worst-case reasoning-interface latency of 279 to 307 ms across input lengths, against a 12 Hz budget of 83.3 ms -- exceeded throughout by three to four times -- while the two-to-six-token interface lands at 38.6 to 66.3 ms and stays within budget at every input length tested.

## Limitations

Stated where it matters. The latency analysis explicitly covers only the reasoning interface and excludes perception preprocessing, trajectory postprocessing and full-stack scheduling overhead, so the budget comparison is about the component under study rather than about a deployed system. The ablation split is marked as not numerically comparable with the main results table, which prevents the most likely misreading. Not stated but worth noticing: all results are open-loop, so nothing here measures what happens when the policy's own errors compound over a closed loop, which is the regime the real-time framing is about. The token vocabulary is designed by hand and its coverage bounds what the reasoning can express -- a situation requiring a manoeuvre outside the vocabulary has no representation, and no analysis of vocabulary coverage or of out-of-vocabulary behaviour is reported. The automatic Reason-Action supervision infers intent from what was logged, so it encodes the demonstrated behaviour as the correct reason, and a systematically suboptimal driving log would teach systematically suboptimal reasoning without that being visible in the metrics. Single runs throughout, no seeds or intervals, and the reinforcement-learning refinement is described as optional but its separate contribution is not isolated in the tables reported here.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-training**: The interesting training claim is that the supervision for the reasoning tokens is derived rather than authored: logged trajectories supply what was done and scene context supplies why, so a Reason-Action pair falls out of driving logs at scale with no annotation. That is the same move the archive's other verified-supervision entries make -- deriving the label from a structure you already control rather than paying someone to write it -- and it comes with the same inherited weakness, which here is specific and worth stating: the intent is inferred from the demonstrated behaviour, so the logs define what counts as correct reasoning, and systematically suboptimal driving would teach systematically suboptimal reasons without that being visible in displacement error. The controlled comparison is the more transferable result. On the same backbone, verbose natural-language reasoning improves longitudinal accuracy while making lateral accuracy worse than no reasoning at all, continuous latent tokens land between, and a fixed executable vocabulary is best on both. So the effect of adding a reasoning interface is not one number: it helped one component of the task and hurt another, and reporting a single aggregate would have shown verbose reasoning as a modest improvement. The ablation localises this cleanly -- the executable tokens buy 18.3 and 25.1 percent on lateral metrics while leaving longitudinal fractionally worse -- which supports reading the mechanism as route-conditioned intent rather than as better trajectory generation generally. Pair this with the archive's other evidence that added reasoning structure is inert unless something supervises what occupies it: here the slots are few, typed, and supervised against logged actions, which is about as constrained as such an interface can get.
- **test-time-scaling**: This is the archive's clearest case of a hard external budget deciding the design rather than accuracy alone. Inter-token decoding costs 3.25 ms, a verbose rationale of 40 to 80 tokens gives 279 to 307 ms of worst-case reasoning latency, and the 12 Hz control loop allows 83.3 ms -- so verbose chain of thought is not merely expensive here but structurally inadmissible, exceeding the budget by three to four times at every input length. The response is not to shorten the rationale but to change what a reasoning step is: a fixed vocabulary of executable manoeuvre tokens, two to six of them, which bounds the length by construction rather than by truncation or a budget-forcing rule applied afterwards. That is a different point on the compression spectrum from the archive's latent-reasoning entries, which replace tokens with continuous states, and the comparison is run here on the same backbone -- with continuous latent tokens landing between verbose reasoning and the executable vocabulary on every metric. Worth carrying: when the budget is externally fixed rather than a cost to be traded against accuracy, the useful question becomes what representation fits inside it, and a discrete typed vocabulary is a third option alongside shorter text and continuous latents. The authors are careful about the scope of their own latency claim, noting it covers only the reasoning interface and excludes perception, postprocessing and scheduling -- so it establishes that the interface fits, not that the system does.

## Abstract

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can connect scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and trajectory generation for autonomous driving. However, verbose natural-language Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is poorly suited to real-time control because it is open-ended, costly to decode, and difficult to optimize as an action-facing representation. We propose XCoT-VLA, which replaces descriptive rationales with compact executable CoT tokens learned from automatically constructed Reason-Action supervision. Logged trajectories provide action evidence, while scene context supplies causal semantics. The predicted XCoT sequence remains in context and conditions fixed trajectory queries through shared multimodal self-attention. Deterministic token-function routing applies the Reason FFN to XCoT tokens and the Control FFN to trajectory queries for flow-matching trajectory generation. We further introduce XCoT Policy Optimization (XCPO) as an optional refinement extension in the same executable token space. XCoT-VLA reduces longitudinal ADE from 1.645 to 1.323 on a general-distribution set and lateral FDE from 1.616 to 0.648 in lane-change scenarios. By representing driving-oriented reasoning with only 2-6 executable XCoT tokens, our method substantially reduces autoregressive reasoning overhead and remains within the real-time planning budget. These results demonstrate that driving-oriented reasoning can be compact, executable, and directly connected to trajectory generation.
